title: Extending the theory of planned behaviour to explain contract cheating in the age of generative AI: evidence from Australian higher education
text_snippet: Extending the theory of planned behaviour to explain contract cheating in the age of generative AI: evidence from Australian higher education Abstract Academic contract cheating (CC) poses a significant challenge for Higher Education (HE), a problem that has become more complex with the increasing use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) tools. While similarity detection software can flag AI-generated text, it remains ineffective in identifying CC, potentially displacing misconduct rather than reducing it. Drawing on and extending the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), this study examines how traditional TPB constructs and technology-mediated perceptual factors jointly influence students’ intentions and behaviours related to CC within the Australian HE context. The findings reveal significant direct and indirect pathways linking perceived instructor involvement, detection awareness, AI-related risk perceptions, and perceived behavioural control to students’ intentions and behaviours. These results extend the TPB framework to the context of AI-mediated academic misconduct and offer practical implications for universities in Australia and potentially other similar contexts. title: Design and validation of an integrated digital storytelling–problem-based learning system in primary mathematics: effects on conceptual understanding of decimal fractions
text_snippet: Design and validation of an integrated digital storytelling–problem-based learning system in primary mathematics: effects on conceptual understanding of decimal fractions Abstract This study investigates the design and empirical validation of an integrated digital storytelling–problem-based learning (PBL) environment for supporting primary students’ conceptual understanding of decimal fractions. Decimal learning remains conceptually demanding due to students’ reliance on whole-number reasoning and difficulty coordinating symbolic and magnitude-based representations. Grounded in multimedia learning theory and inquiry-based pedagogy, the intervention operationalized digital storytelling as a structured multimodal construction process embedded within collaborative problem solving, positioning technology as a representational and cognitive regulation system rather than a presentation medium. A two-phase quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group design was implemented to evaluate both effectiveness and stability of the instructional model. Phase 1 included 66 Grade 5 students in one school, followed by a replication phase with 121 students across two additional schools to examine cross-context robustness. title: Investigating the impact of learning modes and instructional sequences of VR-integrated station activities on science learning from the multimodal perspective
text_snippet: Investigating the impact of learning modes and instructional sequences of VR-integrated station activities on science learning from the multimodal perspective Abstract This study explores the impact of different VR learning modes (direct vs. vicarious) and instructional sequences (VR-Reading vs. Reading-VR) on middle school students’ science learning outcomes and transmodal moments during VR-integrated station activities. Using a mixed-methods design, the research involved 85 seventh-grade students, including multilingual learners (MLs) and English-first-language learners (EFLLs), who participated in a week-long unit on science lab safety and equipment. A 2 × 2 × 2 quasi-experimental design was employed to examine the effects of VR learning modes or instructional sequences across learner types on science learning outcomes. In parallel, multimodal interaction analysis was conducted on video data from 16 focal participants to examine transmodal moments—instances in which meaning shifted across communicative modes and activities—and their associations with learning outcomes. Quantitative analysis revealed that the direct learning mode resulted in significantly higher knowledge gains compared to the vicarious learning mode. title: Implementation of VR learning activities for assessment purposes in teacher education: an evaluation approach using converging item response tree models
text_snippet: Implementation of VR learning activities for assessment purposes in teacher education: an evaluation approach using converging item response tree models Abstract Although virtual reality (VR) classroom simulations are recognised as an effective way of promoting teaching skills, they are rarely used for assessment purposes in teacher training. This study examines an analysis strategy rooted in Item Response Tree (IRTree) modelling for estimating the psychometric quality of VR classroom simulations and to identify its implications for designing VR classroom simulations in teacher education, thereby making explicit how the structural properties of a VR classroom simulation determine the requirements of its psychometric evaluation. Data from 200 student teachers who participated in the VR classroom simulation CLASIVIR 1.0 were analysed. The results revealed good model fit and stable estimates, demonstrating a high level of measurement accuracy and strong potential of IRTree models replicating the expected structures of psychological constructs. Thus, the applicability of the proposed analysis strategy was proven, indicating that CLASIVIR 1.0 can be used to reliably measure classroom management competence. title: Exploring student use of generative AI in higher education: A dual-institutional study
text_snippet: Exploring student use of generative AI in higher education: A dual-institutional study Abstract Although a growing body of research has examined students’ attitudes toward generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, few studies have compared perceptions across contrasting institutional contexts or explored how students’ reported uses of GenAI relate to broader learning practices. This study addresses that gap by examining university students’ perceptions, self-reported competence, and use of GenAI at two Swedish universities with different academic profiles: a technology-oriented institution and a broader multidisciplinary institution. The study is based on an exploratory questionnaire survey administered to all enrolled students at both universities, yielding 1,097 responses (University A response rate: 11.27%, University B response rate: 14.06%) from students across diverse disciplines, including engineering, nursing, and criminology. title: Performance, interaction, and ethical evaluation in the use of generative artificial intelligence in engineering education
text_snippet: Performance, interaction, and ethical evaluation in the use of generative artificial intelligence in engineering education Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly incorporated into engineering education, particularly in programming courses, raising questions about its effects on learning processes and its acceptability in academic contexts. Empirical evidence examining both interaction patterns and ethical evaluation of Generative artificial intelligence use in real classroom settings remains limited, and studies addressing these dimensions jointly are scarce. This study adopts a multi-phase empirical design to examine student engagement with Generative artificial intelligence across these two complementary dimensions. In Phase 1, a classroom-based activity was conducted with 340 first-year engineering students who completed a time-constrained debugging task using Generative artificial intelligence as the sole external assistance tool. title: When university students’ insecurities drive them to rely excessively on Artificial Intelligence: Relationship between fear of failure, self-esteem, social support and ChatGPT dependence
text_snippet: When university students’ insecurities drive them to rely excessively on Artificial Intelligence: Relationship between fear of failure, self-esteem, social support and ChatGPT dependence Abstract In learning processes, students with a high fear of failure and low self-esteem may be more inclined to use technologies like artificial intelligence (ChatGPT…) to avoid making mistakes, potentially even developing a dependency on such tools. However, it is believed that having peers and teachers who help these students build confidence and receive support to overcome failure could act as a buffer against attachment to technological tools like ChatGPT. To test this hypothesis, 467 university students participated by completing a series of scales to measure their fear of failure, self-esteem, peer support, teacher support, and dependency on ChatGPT. Following a moderated mediation analysis, the results revealed that the initial hypothesis was not supported. Indeed, higher levels of fear of failure and lower levels of self-esteem did not lead to an increase in ChatGPT dependence. Likewise, social support from peers and teachers did not influence the previously mentioned relationship.

text_snippet: The impact of place-based local contexts, presence, and narrative design on headset virtual reality engagement and learning in non-formal education settings Abstract While virtual reality (VR) learning experiences have been widely studied in formal educational settings, fewer studies have explored their impact in non-formal environments across diverse age groups. This study used path analysis to examine how place-based local context, immersion, presence, and VR design features (narrative, guidance and feedback) predict participants’ engagement, industrial history content knowledge, affective learning, and perceptions of local environmental learning. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was also conducted to explore differences by age, gender, race, and watershed residence. Results indicated a statistically significant increase in content knowledge from pretest to posttest, with no significant group differences for gender, race, or residence across outcome variables. Path analysis findings highlighted the importance of presence and local context for engagement and affective learning. title: The 3D4E strategic approach: Can GAI improve visual thinking skills in STEM high schools?
text_snippet: The 3D4E strategic approach: Can GAI improve visual thinking skills in STEM high schools? Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) has the potential to transform education, particularly in fostering students’ visual thinking skills (VTS) within STEM learning. However, its pedagogical value depends on strategic integration guided by cognitive and instructional principles. This study introduces the 3D4E Strategic Approach—a structured model encompassing Define, Design, Develop, Evaluate, and Enhance phases—to optimize the educational use of GAI visualization tools for improving VTS among STEM high school students. Grounded in Whole Brain Theory (WBT) and Brain-Based Learning Theory (BBLT), the approach operationalizes iterative cycles that engage both hemispheres of the brain to promote conceptual understanding and creative visualization. A quasi-experimental design was employed in a STEM high school with an experimental and a control group. Data was collected using a cognitive VTS test and an observational performance rubric. title: Storytelling and educational robotics in literature education: a quasi-experimental study
text_snippet: Storytelling and educational robotics in literature education: a quasi-experimental study Abstract Despite the growing interest in integrating educational robotics into storytelling activities, only a few empirical studies have been conducted in the field of literature education. Accordingly, the present study examines the integration of Storytelling and Educational Robotics into the teaching of Greek literature (Homer’s Odyssey), in comparison with conventional Storytelling -based instruction. The study was conducted over 16 weeks in five public secondary schools in Greece with 227 participants aged 12–13 and employed a quasi-experimental design involving an experimental group (156 students) and a control group (71 students). The experimental group received an 8-lesson storytelling-robotics course using the DuckyCode robot. The control group received the same literary content through conventional instruction. The learning outcomes for both groups were measured on three different occasions: prior to the start of the intervention (pre-test), during the intervention (intermediate test), and after the completion of the intervention (post-test). title: Interactive learning dashboards: rethinking learning visualisations as engagement tools
text_snippet: Interactive learning dashboards: rethinking learning visualisations as engagement tools Abstract Learning Analytics Dashboards (LADs) have shown limited impact on student outcomes, often functioning as static visualizations. In this paper, we present a case study reimagining LADs as interactive tools that promote student engagement. Namely, we extend a conventional LAD with a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered pedagogical agent and an interactive Judgement of Learning (JoL) feature to support students’ awareness of their study progress. The pedagogical agent engaged students in conversations about their learning data, while the JoL feature required self-assessment before viewing system metrics, encouraging learners’ calibration of their judgement. This interactive LAD (ILAD) was implemented in a university programming course with three randomly assigned conditions: no agent, a “telling” agent providing information about learner data, and an “eliciting” agent asking questions about learner data. The case study reports on the data collected over five weeks from thirty students paid to regularly use the ILAD within their computer science course. title: Curating flexible learning spaces in museums with a virtual reality application
text_snippet: Curating flexible learning spaces in museums with a virtual reality application Abstract This study explores how pre-service teachers conceptualise and experience the design of flexible learning spaces in museums using Virtual Reality (VR). Grounded in phenomenological methodology and informed by Lefebvre (1991) spatial triad, it examines how immersive digital environments foster spatial literacy, pedagogical creativity, and professional identity. Participants enrolled in a Primary education programme engaged in a four-phase VR-based activity in which they designed a modular museum learning environment using Oculus Rift headsets. Data from pre- and post-activity reflections reveal that VR translated abstract educational theories into practical design decisions and stimulated emotional connections to the learning environment. Findings suggest that immersive environments foster embodied cognition and serve as catalyst tools for teacher education. Participants reported increased confidence in designing inclusive and adaptive learning environments and enthusiasm for integrating immersive tools into educational practice. title: From marginalization to empowerment: Investigating the role of digital technology in reducing social exclusion for children with disabilities in Egyptian schools
text_snippet: From marginalization to empowerment: Investigating the role of digital technology in reducing social exclusion for children with disabilities in Egyptian schools Abstract While digital technology is widely promoted as a catalyst for inclusive education, its benefits for children with disabilities remain uneven in low- and middle-income countries. Guided by an integrated theoretical framework encompassing empowerment theory, social capital, and universal design for learning (UDL), this convergent mixed-methods study examined how digital and assistive technologies are perceived to influence educational participation, social inclusion, and empowerment for children with disabilities in Egypt, with specific attention to rural-urban disparities. Survey data were collected from 314 teachers across schools serving learners with visual, hearing, and physical disabilities, complemented by six parent focus groups. Quantitative results indicated generally positive perceptions of educational impact and attitudes toward digital inclusion, alongside moderate ratings of accessibility and social inclusion and persistent constraints related to infrastructure and support.
